value.overview: The Great Frigatebird (Fregata minor) is a large, highly aerial seabird of tropical oceans. It has extremely long, narrow wings, a deeply forked tail, and a long hooked bill. Males are mostly black with a bright red throat pouch, while females usually have dark upperparts and a white breast and belly. It spends much of its life over the open sea and returns to remote tropical islands to breed. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon offshore visitor and is easily confused with the more widespread Magnificent Frigatebird.
value.classification: The Great Frigatebird belongs to the frigatebird family Fregatidae and the order Suliformes. Its scientific name is Fregata minor.
value.identification: This species is recognized by its very large size, long angular wings, deeply forked tail, and effortless soaring flight. Adult males are largely black, often showing a greenish or purplish sheen, with a conspicuous red inflatable throat pouch during courtship. Females have a dark head and back with a contrasting white breast and belly. Juveniles have a pale head and breast. In Costa Rica, careful identification is important because Magnificent Frigatebirds are much more commonly encountered and can look similar at a distance.
value.rangeHabitat: The Great Frigatebird has a broad pantropical distribution, breeding on remote islands in the Indian and Pacific oceans and in the eastern Pacific, including the Galápagos. It uses open tropical seas, coastal waters, oceanic upwellings, and offshore islands, usually roosting or nesting in trees and shrubs on predator-free islands. In Costa Rica it is not a regular breeding species; it occurs mainly as an uncommon or rare visitor over Pacific waters and near offshore areas, with occasional records along the Pacific coast. It is much scarcer than the Magnificent Frigatebird.
value.migrationStatus: The species is not a conventional long-distance migrant. It disperses widely from breeding colonies and makes seasonal or weather-related movements over tropical oceans. In Costa Rica, individuals are best treated as irregular, nonbreeding Pacific visitors rather than a predictable migrant or resident population.
value.breeding: Great Frigatebirds breed colonially on remote tropical islands, often in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or low vegetation. The nest is a platform of sticks, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the single chick. Breeding colonies may be used repeatedly, but reproduction is slow and young birds remain dependent for a long period. Courtship includes males inflating their red throat pouches and displaying their wings and bills. Costa Rica has no known major breeding colony of this species.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of flying fish, squid, and other marine animals taken near the sea surface. Great Frigatebirds often feed around tuna, dolphins, and other predators that drive fish upward. They also seize prey from the water or capture food near fishing activity. A notable behavior is kleptoparasitism: the frigatebird chases gulls, terns, boobies, and other seabirds until they drop or regurgitate their food, which it catches in flight.
value.behavior: Great Frigatebirds are superb fliers and can soar for hours on thermals and wind currents with little wing flapping. They may travel far from land while foraging and can remain airborne for extended periods. They usually avoid landing on the water because their plumage is not well suited to swimming. Birds gather at roosts and breeding colonies, while males defend small display areas during courtship. Offshore sightings in Costa Rica may involve solitary birds or small groups moving along productive coastal waters.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, but the magnitude and causes of the overall trend are not well quantified. Regional colonies may show different patterns.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include disturbance at breeding colonies, loss or degradation of nesting habitat, introduced predators on islands, human harvest in some regions, marine pollution, entanglement or interactions with fishing activities, and changes in food availability. Because Great Frigatebirds depend on remote islands and productive ocean areas, pressures affecting both nesting sites and marine ecosystems can reduce breeding success and survival.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remote island nesting colonies and prevent introduced rats, cats, pigs, and other predators from reaching breeding sites. Reduce disturbance around colonies, support sustainable fisheries and efforts to limit seabird bycatch, and reduce marine plastic and other pollution. In Costa Rica, report unusual sightings with photographs and precise locations, especially from offshore waters, while avoiding disturbance to resting or nesting seabirds.
